newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-Merrill dismisses Indian recession fears.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Merrill dismisses Indian recession fears.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch on Wednesday shrugged off growing fears of a recession in the Indian economy and said it expected a reversal of the temporary slowdown in coming months.
"It is very difficult to characterise the current slowdown as a recession," John Praveen, senior international economist at Merrill, told Reuters in an interview.
India's 24-sector industrial production index rose just 5.6 percent during April-August 1996 against 12.6 percent a year ago, the Industry Ministry said on Tuesday.

Falling imports and exports, declining demand for consumer goods, listless primary and secondary equity markets and high interest rates have all contributed to the theory India might be headed for a recession.
Praveen said it was possible the current slowdown was being exaggerated to bring pressure on India's central bank to ease monetary conditions.
"What better way than to raise the spectre of recession?," he said. The Reserve Bank of India is due to announce its credit policy for the second half of 1996/97 (April-March) on Saturday.
Bankers expect the RBI to cut cash reserve requirements of banks injecting liquidity into the market and sparking a fall in interest rates.

"We expect things to turnaround in the next couple of months. The slowdown is a temporary blip," Praveen said, adding expected recoveries for Japan and Europe -- which account for 34 percent of India's exports -- would help matters.
Praveen said growth in the economy was solid with inflation trending down. Downward pressure was being exerted on interest rates and current account deficit was at sustainable levels.
"We were a little nervous as it became clearer no single party would form the government but the new government made an immediate, explicit commitment to reduce the deficit," he said.

India's 13-party ruling coalition United Front came to power in June. In a common minimum programme outlining its economic policies the government said it would reduce fiscal deficit to 4.0 percent of GDP from 5.9 percent in 1995/96.
Praveen said a key macro policy reform was a 1994 decision to phase out by 1997/98 the system of automatic monetisation of the budget deficit through the issue of ad hoc treasury bills.

Though India's GDP growth is lower than the Asian tiger economies, its current account deficits are smaller than those in other emerging markets in Asia and Latin America. Inflation in India is low compared to inflation in Latin America and on par with inflation in other Asian countries, he said.

Praveen said infrastructure deficiencies and bottlenecks are likely to be a major constraint to growth but the challenge of the country's infrastructure needs would provide a major opportunity for foreign investment.
